article.title: What Color Undertones Do I Have? 5 Easy Tests to Find Out
article.meta_description: Not sure if you're cool, warm, neutral or olive? Try five simple at-home undertone tests, learn how to read mixed results, and see which colors to try.
article.h1: What Color Undertones Do I Have? 5 Simple Tests to Find Out
article.body_html:
Your undertone is the subtle, steady hue beneath your skin's surface color, and it generally falls into one of four groups: cool, warm, neutral or olive. You can work out your likely undertone at home with a few quick checks in natural light, then count your results instead of trusting any single test. Treat the answer as a styling starting point, not a rule.

Undertone in 30 seconds: what it is and why it matters

Undertone is the hue under the surface of your skin. It is what makes a certain lipstick look fresh on you and another look slightly off, or why one white shirt looks crisp while another looks a bit harsh near your face. Knowing it narrows down the colors to try first, which saves time when you shop for clothes, jewelry and makeup.

Undertone vs. surface skin tone (and why a tan doesn't change it)

Skin tone (often called depth) is how light or deep your skin looks overall. Undertone is the hue underneath that. Two people can have the same depth and different undertones. A tan or a flush of redness changes the surface, but the underlying hue is generally considered stable. That is why a tan can make you misread your result. If you want to sort out depth separately, see our guide What Is My Skin Tone?

The four labels you'll see: cool, warm, neutral, olive

  • Cool: a pink, rosy or bluish cast underneath.
  • Warm: a yellow, peachy or golden cast underneath.
  • Neutral: a fairly even balance of cool and warm, with neither clearly winning.
  • Olive: a muted, slightly greenish or grayish-gold cast, usually with some warmth mixed in.

Set up first so you read your skin fairly

Most wrong answers come from poor conditions, not poor skin-reading. Spend two minutes on setup before any test.

Use natural daylight, near a window, with no filters

Stand facing a window in daytime. Avoid warm yellow bulbs, cool LED strips and direct harsh sun, which all shift how skin looks. If you check with a phone camera, turn off beauty filters and automatic skin smoothing.

Go bare-faced and take off colored clothing and bold jewelry

Remove foundation, tinted moisturizer and blush if you can. Wear a plain white or neutral top, and move away from brightly painted walls, which can bounce color onto your face.

Why redness, a fresh tan or colored lighting can mislead you

Temporary flushing can make a warm or neutral person look cool and pink. A fresh tan can make a cool person look golden. If either applies, test the skin on the inner arm or an area that sees less sun, and consider re-checking in a few weeks. This is cosmetic reading only. If you have any concern about your skin itself, ask a doctor or dermatologist.

5 simple tests to find your undertone

Do all five and jot down a result for each: cool, warm, neutral or unsure. No single test is conclusive.

Test 1: The vein test (and its limits)

Look at the inside of your wrist in daylight. Veins that look bluish or purple lean cool. Veins that look greenish or olive lean warm. If you see both, note "neutral." The limits: vein color is affected by depth of skin, lighting and how close the vein sits to the surface, so many people honestly cannot tell. Count it as a weak vote.

Test 2: The gold vs. silver jewelry test

Hold a gold piece and a silver piece against your bare skin, one near the jaw and one near the other. Which makes your skin look brighter and healthier? Silver often flatters cool undertones, gold often flatters warm ones, and neutral skin tends to look fine in both. Rose gold sits in between and often suits cool and neutral skin.

Test 3: The white vs. off-white fabric test

Hold a stark, bright white fabric against your face, then a cream or ivory one. If bright white looks crisp and cream looks slightly dull or yellow on you, you may lean cool. If cream looks rich and bright white feels harsh, you may lean warm. If both work, note neutral.

Test 4: How your skin looks next to different colors

Hold solid pieces under your chin, one at a time. Compare pairs such as:

  • Icy pink vs. peach
  • Royal blue vs. camel
  • Emerald vs. olive green
  • Burgundy vs. rust

If the first of each pair makes your face look clearer and more even, vote cool. If the second does, vote warm. If the shadows under your eyes and jaw look softer in one set, that set is probably closer to your undertone.

Test 5: Which foundation or concealer shades seem to vanish into your skin

If you own a few shades, swatch them along your jawline in daylight. The one that disappears is the closest match. Pink or rosy bases that blend suggest cool, yellow or golden bases suggest warm, and a mix of both suggests neutral. Bases with a slightly muted, greenish-gold look that blend often point toward olive. Remember that product undertone labels vary by brand, so compare the result with your other tests.

Add up your results: cool, warm, neutral or olive

A simple tally: how to read your answers

  1. Write down your vote from each of the five tests.
  2. Count cool, warm and neutral/unsure votes.
  3. If one group has three or more votes, that is your likely undertone.
  4. If votes are split evenly or you keep writing "both," read the neutral and olive notes below.

What a neutral undertone looks like in practice

Neutral means your skin carries both cool and warm hues without one clearly leading. In practice, you might look good in both gold and silver, find that both bright white and cream work, and see greenish-blue veins. You often have a wider range to play with, and the details (depth and contrast) will steer your choices more than undertone does.

What olive undertone means and how it differs from neutral

Olive is a distinct case, not just a synonym for warm. It usually looks muted, with a slight green or gray-gold cast. Olive skin can look dull or sallow next to very pink or very orange shades, and it often does well with earthy, saturated colors such as emerald, deep teal, rust and warm burgundy. Neutral is a balanced mix, while olive has that specific greenish, muted quality. If your tests are mixed and you notice that muted cast, olive may be the better label.

When your tests disagree: which ones to trust less

Trust the vein test least, because lighting and vessel depth affect it. Give more weight to the color-against-face comparison (Test 4) and the fabric test, because they show you how colors actually behave near your face, which is what matters for styling. If you are still torn, choose "neutral" for now and rely on what looks best in the mirror.

What colors tend to flatter each undertone

These are common starting points, not strict lists.

Clothing colors for cool, warm, neutral and olive undertones

UndertoneColors to try firstAn easy pairing
CoolNavy, royal blue, emerald, plum, icy pink, charcoal, true redNavy blazer, white tee, gray trousers
WarmCamel, olive, rust, terracotta, mustard, coral, creamCream knit, camel coat, rust scarf
NeutralSoft white, dusty rose, teal, taupe, medium blues and greensTeal top, taupe trousers, soft white sneakers
OliveEmerald, deep teal, forest green, rust, warm burgundy, camelForest green shirt, tan chinos, brown loafers

For more on combining colors across an outfit, our guide to color matching clothes covers pairings in depth.

Jewelry and metal tones

Cool: silver, platinum, white gold. Warm: yellow gold, brass, copper. Neutral: gold, silver or rose gold, or mixed metals. Olive: antique or yellow gold often looks rich, but silver can work if the piece is bold and clean.

Makeup: foundation, blush and lipstick starting points

  • Cool: foundation with a pink or neutral-pink base, rose or berry blush, blue-red or raspberry lipstick.
  • Warm: golden or peachy foundation, peach or apricot blush, coral, brick or warm red lipstick.
  • Neutral: balanced foundation, soft rose or peach blush, mauve or rosy-nude lipstick.
  • Olive: foundation with a slight golden-olive balance, warm terracotta or soft coral blush, brick, deep berry or warm nude lipstick.

For shape and feature guidance beyond color, try the What Makeup Suits My Face? quiz.

Colors outside your "palette": how to wear them with confidence

You can wear any color you love. A few tricks help:

  • Placement: put a tricky color on the bottom half, such as trousers, a skirt or shoes, and keep a flattering color near your face.
  • A flattering layer near the face: a neutral tee, scarf or necklace between the color and your skin softens the effect.
  • Adjust the shade: if bright orange is harsh on you, try a deeper rust. If icy pink looks washed out, try a dusty rose.
  • Use makeup as a bridge: a lip or blush color that echoes the garment can tie it together.

Undertone is a starting point, not a rulebook

Why contrast level, depth and personal taste matter too

Undertone is one factor among several. Contrast (how different your hair, skin and eyes are from one another) affects whether you suit bold color blocking or softer, tonal looks. Depth affects how rich or pale a color can be before it overwhelms you. And preference counts: if a color makes you feel great, it is working.

Skin depth is a separate question

Depth and undertone are different questions, and both matter for choosing foundation or deciding how light or deep a color should be. Our skin tone guide covers depth in full, so you can combine it with what you learned here.

Using a camera-based tool as a second opinion

After your own tests, a camera-based tool can offer another view to compare with your tally. The Live skin analysis in the FitCheck AI Android app gives an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions, and you can read more on the live skin analysis page. It is AI opinion, not professional color analysis, and it does not replace your own tests or a mirror check.

How to take a photo that gives a fairer read

Face natural light near a window, hold the camera at eye level, and turn off any filters. Remove colored tops or wear a neutral one, and skip heavy makeup so the camera sees as little added color as possible.

How to compare an AI overview with your own tests

Write down your five-test tally first, then check what the tool suggests. If they agree, you have more confidence. If they differ, repeat the setup in better light and try the color-against-face test again. When you try on an outfit, Live FitCheck can also give color analysis and matching suggestions, which helps you see how a specific color works for you in practice.

Not medical advice: cosmetic guidance only

The AI feedback is cosmetic style guidance only and is not medical advice, so please see a dermatologist or doctor for any concern about your skin.

faqs.question: Can my undertone change over time?
faqs.answer: Your undertone is generally considered stable, but how your skin looks can shift. Tanning, redness, and changes in hair color can make it seem like your undertone has changed, so re-test in natural light with a bare face before deciding. If you notice skin changes that worry you, speak to a doctor or dermatologist.

faqs.question: Can I have a different undertone on my face and body?
faqs.answer: It can look that way, since the face often has more redness and sun exposure than the rest of the body. For choosing colors near your face, go with what you see on your face and neck in daylight. For body makeup or self-tanner, check a less sun-exposed area such as the inner arm.

faqs.question: Is neutral the same as olive?
faqs.answer: No. Neutral means your cool and warm hues are fairly balanced. Olive usually has a muted, slightly greenish or gray-gold cast with some warmth. The two can be hard to tell apart, so compare how emerald, rust and dusty rose look next to your face.

faqs.question: Do I have to avoid colors that aren't in my undertone's palette?
faqs.answer: No. Undertone is a starting point, and personal taste matters just as much. If you love a color that isn't on your list, wear it away from your face, add a flattering layer near your neckline, or try a slightly deeper or softer version of the shade.

faqs.question: Which test is the most reliable?
faqs.answer: No single test is reliable on its own. The color-against-face comparison and the fabric test are usually more helpful than the vein test, because they show how colors actually look near your face. The best approach is to run several tests and go with the result that appears most often.

review.notes: This is a strong, practical, well-structured informational article. It directly answers the query with five tests, a tally method, a section on mixed results, and palettes. Its caveats are honest: no single test is conclusive, undertone is a starting point, and the app output is AI opinion. It contains no invented stats, studies or testimonials. The medical referrals are appropriate. The problem is the app tie-in, which implies the skin analysis or Live FitCheck can assess or confirm undertone. Fix by reframing the app section as optional cosmetic suggestions and outfit color matching, rewording the CTA, and removing wording that has the tool 'agreeing' or 'differing' with undertone results. Also fix the Test 2 sentence and clarify how unsure votes are handled in the tally. Minor: some people treat olive as a subtype of neutral or warm, so a brief note that labels vary would help.
